adherence.reason: The piece is clearly framed as historical fiction, using an imagined artisan and ceremony in an Aztec-era setting.
Teotl is the protagonist and is shown crafting a ceremonial feather headdress for the noble Lord Itzcoatl.
The narrative repeatedly and explicitly locates the workshop and ceremony in Tenochtitlan.
Rare feathers are supplied by traders who travel for months to the city markets, but the featherworker is written as male rather than the required woman.
The work takes place in the final three days and then the morning of the named Great Festival of New Fire.
Teotl secretly weaves a protective jaguar-eye symbol into the headdress despite the priests' explicit ban on hidden symbols.
The required exact lowercase phrase ending with a period never appears; the closest instance begins with capitalized 'Every' and ends with a comma.
The final scene has Lord Itzcoatl wearing the headdress while remaining unaware of the hidden jaguar-eye symbol.
